question: Is a journal required for traditional (paper, in-person) notarizations in Florida?

options.text: Not by statute for most paper acts, but it's strongly recommended
options.why: Correct. Chapter 117 requires journals for online notarizations; for most paper acts a journal isn't mandated but is strongly recommended.
Wrong. Thumbprint journals are a California requirement, not Florida's.
Wrong. Journals aren't banned; the Governor's manual encourages them.
Wrong. There's no rule limiting journals to marriages.

explanation: Florida requires journals for online notarizations; for traditional acts, keeping one is recommended.
source: Fla. Stat. §117.245; Governor's Reference Manual for Notaries

refs.title: Governor's Reference Manual for Notaries: Keeping Records via a Notary Journal (p. 12)

question: How long must an online notary keep the electronic journal?

options.why: Correct. §117.245 requires online notaries to keep the electronic journal for at least ten years.
Wrong. Five years is the Texas rule.
Wrong. One year is far too short.
Wrong. Retention runs well past the commission.

explanation: Online notaries keep their electronic journal for at least ten years.

question: How long must an online notary keep the audio-video recording?

options.why: Correct. §117.245 requires recordings to be kept at least ten years.
Wrong. 90 days is far too short.
Wrong. Two years is too short.
Wrong. Ten years is the minimum; the statute doesn't say forever.

explanation: Recordings must be kept at least ten years.

question: Why keep a journal even when not required?

options.text: It documents what the notary did and protects the notary and public
options.why: Correct. A journal is evidence of what the notary did, protecting the notary and the public.
Wrong. Fees are capped regardless of record keeping.
Wrong. Identification is always required.
Wrong. Selling journal data would be a misuse of personal information.

explanation: A journal is evidence of proper procedure.

refs.title: Governor's Reference Manual for Notaries: Keeping Records via a Notary Journal (p. 12)

question: Which item belongs in an online notary's journal entry?

options.text: Date and time, type of act, the principal's name and address, how identity was verified, and the fee
options.why: Correct. §117.245 requires these items, among others, in each online journal entry.
Wrong. A notary should never collect a principal's password.
Wrong. Financial details like bank balances have nothing to do with the notarization.

options.text: A copy of the full document text
options.why: Wrong. The journal records the act, not a copy of the document's text.

explanation: Online journal entries include date and time, type of act, principal details, identification method and fee.

question: May an online notary use a third-party custodian for records?

options.text: Yes, a qualified secure repository may hold them, but the notary remains responsible
options.why: Correct. Florida allows a qualified secure repository to hold online records, but the notary remains responsible for them.
Wrong. Third-party custodians are allowed.

options.text: Yes, and the notary is no longer responsible
options.why: Wrong. Using a custodian doesn't shift the legal duty away from the notary.

options.text: Only the signer may hold them
options.why: Wrong. Principals don't keep the notary's official records.

explanation: Records may be kept by a qualified secure repository, but the notary remains responsible.

question: When should a journal entry be made?

options.text: At the time of the notarial act
options.why: Correct. Entries made at the time of the act are complete and accurate.
Wrong. Monthly entries lose details.
Wrong. Renewal is years later.
Wrong. Every act should be recorded, not only on request.

refs.title: Governor's Reference Manual for Notaries: Keeping Records via a Notary Journal (p. 12)

question: Should a journal include a signer's full Social Security number?

options.why: Correct. Recording Social Security numbers serves no notarial purpose and creates identity-theft risk.
Wrong. It isn't required and is risky.
Wrong. Deeds don't need SSNs in a notary journal.
Wrong. Even a partial SSN serves no notarial purpose.

refs.title: Governor's Reference Manual for Notaries: Keeping Records via a Notary Journal (p. 12)

question: When credible witnesses are used, what record does Florida require?

options.text: The credible witnesses' sworn written statements, which the notary should retain with records
options.why: Correct. Credible witnesses give sworn written statements, which the notary should keep with the record of the act.
Wrong. Florida requires a sworn written statement from credible witnesses.
Wrong. Thumbprints are a California journal rule, not Florida's witness requirement.
Wrong. Tax returns have nothing to do with identifying a signer.

explanation: Credible witnesses give sworn written statements, which should be kept.

question: How should a notary journal be stored?

options.why: Correct. Journals contain personal data and must be kept secure and under the notary's control.
Wrong. An open shelf lets anyone read or alter entries.
Wrong. The journal is the notary's record, not the employer's.
Wrong. Posting it online exposes signers' data.

explanation: Keep journals secure and under the notary's control.

refs.title: Governor's Reference Manual for Notaries: Keeping Records via a Notary Journal (p. 12)

question: An online notary's commission ends. What happens to the 10-year retention duty?

options.text: It continues for the full period
options.why: Correct. The ten-year retention period runs from the act, so it continues after the commission ends.
Wrong. Retention doesn't stop when the commission ends.
Wrong. Signers don't take custody of the notary's records.
Wrong. Destroying records early violates §117.245.

explanation: Records must still be kept for the full retention period.

question: Which identification detail is useful to record?

options.text: The type of ID and its issuer
options.why: Correct. Recording the ID type and issuer documents how identity was established.
Wrong. The ID's color is useless as evidence.
Wrong. Salary is irrelevant and private.
Wrong. Religion is irrelevant and inappropriate to record.

explanation: Record the ID type and issuer.
source: Fla. Stat. §117.245(1)(e); Florida Governor's Notary FAQ
